Data stream processing is a valid research area that considers the data of large volume and high velocity, which makes solutions for data streams adequate for many modern problems [1]. An important factor in processing data streams is the data nonstationarity, resulting from concept drifts [2], which may lead to the loss of the method’s recognition abilities. Finally, Section 7 concludes the work and shows possible future directions. 2 Related works Processing data streams comes with inevitable challenges related to the volume of the data and its temporal nature [16]. One of the most frequently addressed difficulties of this data type is the data nonstationarity, resulting from concept drifts [17]. The significance of recognizing concept changes stems from the fact that they usually harm the recognition quality of methods since the knowledge generalized in machine learning models becomes outdated. The primary axis of the concept drift taxonomy describes its impact on the recognitionmodelor,alternatively,thedatadistributionshiftinrelationtothede- cisionboundary[3].Changesthatdonotaffecttherecognitionquality–andthere- forecannotberecognizedwhenmonitoringthequalityofthemodel–arereferred to as virtual. Meanwhile, those that affect the decision boundary are referred to as real [18]. It is worth keeping in mind that the potentially insignificant virtual changes can be visible in the initial stage of non-sudden real concept changes [19]. The other axes of the concept drift taxonomy consider the drift dynamics and its recurrence. The transition between the consecutive concepts canbesudden –whereonecanseeasingletimeinstantafterwhichthesamples come from the new concept. The other categories describe slower-paced changes in the form of gradual or incremental drifts, in which one can observe a pe- riod of concept transition. In the gradual changes, the samples in the transition period are sampled from both the previous and the emerging concepts, while in the incremental changes, they form a temporary superposition of the two transitioning concepts. Finally, regardless of the dynamics of drift, the concepts thatappearedinthepastmayreoccur,whichistypicaloftheproblemsdescrib- ing the phenomena of cyclic nature [15]. Concept drift detection Sinceconceptchangesmayhavearealeffectonrecogni- tion quality, it has become a standard procedure to monitor the state of a sys- tem in search for a concept drift [20]. For this purpose, many solutions have 4 Joanna Komorniczak been proposed. The initial drift detection methods exploited the fact that con- cept drift affects the classification quality. Those methods include the Adaptive Windowing [21], which uses varying-width windows to compare the frequency of errors. Methods that monitor the quality of a classification model are de- scribed as explicit [22]. The primary benefit of such a drift detection approach is the possibility to directly act upon a change by adapting the classification model to the current data. The use of explicit methods also has some draw- backs. Since their operation is based on recognition quality, the method will not be able to detect the virtual drifts or the initial phases of real ones that do not yetimpactrecognitionquality.Anotherdisadvantageistherelianceontheavail- abilityoflabels,which,inthedatastreamswithhighvelocity,areoftendelayed or not available entirely [8]. Another category of methods monitor characteristics of data stream pro- cessing other than those related to the quality of the model – the implicit drift detection methods. Those include both supervised and unsupervised ap- proaches. The supervised drift detectors can use labels to monitor the quality of the data distribution that are not related to the errors made by the classi- fier. The Centroid Distance Drift Detector [4] is a simple yet effective approach that monitors the class centroids to detect concept changes. Data stream classification The drift detection task remains critical in the area of data stream classification. The proposed drift detection methods can serve as the independent component of a processing pipeline or be integrated with a classifier, forming a hybrid method [31], which has become a standard solu- tion for data stream classification tasks. Data stream classifiers often employ theensemble learning paradigm [14],profitingfromthepossibilityofcontinuous modification of the ensemble’s structure and the possibility of integration with a drift detection module. According to the taxonomy of ensemble methods for data stream classification, the active ones use a drift detection module and di- rectly act upon a change. The other category of passive methods incrementally adapts to the currently processed data, regardless if the concept drift occurred or the data distribution remained stationary. Among the active ensemble approaches, one should mention adwinBagging, whichusedanAdaptive Windowing driftdetectorcombinedwithonline bagging to enable the incremental learning of classifier pool and modification of the en- semble structure when the concept drift is detected [32]. Most of the methods utilized the monitoring of classification accuracy. Meanwhile, there exist en- semble approaches that, similarly to implicit drift detectors, base their detec- tion on other factors unrelated to the classification quality. One such method is the Covariance-signature Concept Selector [33], which examines the covari- ance of the features to detect concept changes and to select the best model for current data distribution. A similar strategy was used in the already mentioned ficsum [28], which selects the classifier dedicated to the currently solved task based on the gathered meta-information. The av- eraged results are presented in Figure 3, showing the value of normalized mu- tual information between clusters describing the concepts in the data stream and the concept ground-truth, describing the actual concept. As expected, the task of concept clustering is becoming more difficult with a smaller number of samples in the data chunk. It can result from less accurate frequency component selection or the generation of less diverse frequency repre- sentation of data. Therefore, when possible, selecting a larger chunk size should allow for a more precise data stream description. Similarly, the task becomes more difficult when the number of concept drifts rises. The growing number of concepts while the data stream length remains constant results in fewer sam- ples describing each cluster. This can result in less accurate frequency selection or increase the complexity of the clustering task, where the number of formed clusters increases. JSON: Name: ffm_frequency_metadescriptor Title: Frequency-filtering metadescriptor for unsupervised concept identification in nonstationary high-dimensional data streams Short Hypothesis: Selecting the top-n frequency components by across-batch variance from chunk-level Fourier transforms and clustering those representations yields higher unsupervised concept identification performance than PCA and common meta-feature sets on high-dimensional nonstationary data streams. Related Work: Existing concept-drift and data-stream metadescription approaches fall into two broad families: explicit detectors that monitor classifier error and implicit detectors that monitor alternative data or model statistics (centroid movement, margin density, complexity measures). Other strategies construct meta-feature vectors per chunk using statistical aggregates (means, variances, skewness, kurtosis, entropy, discriminant ratios) and apply clustering or selection; these meta-feature sets can be computed incrementally but often scale poorly or require many hand-designed features. Dimensionality reduction baselines such as PCA provide compact representations but lack interpretable, reconstructible semantic components. Frequency-based analyses in the literature have primarily targeted temporal patterns across time for specific features rather than per-sample spatial feature correlations; they do not address chunk-level frequency selection for per-sample feature vectors. Limitations across prior methods include reliance on labels or classifier outputs, poor scaling or instability with very high feature dimensionality, limited semantic interpretability of components, and inadequate support for post-hoc concept identification and visualization. Abstract: We address unsupervised post-hoc identification and visualization of concepts in nonstationary, high-dimensional data streams. We propose a Frequency-Filtering Metadescriptor that computes chunk-level Fourier transforms of per-sample feature vectors, averages sample-level spectra per chunk, ranks frequency components by variance across chunks, and retains the top-n components as a compact metadescription. Optionally, the retained frequency vectors are clustered to identify concepts and inverted to visualize representative spatial patterns. The method leverages frequency-domain generalization to compress inter-feature dependencies into a small interpretable set of components while remaining label-agnostic and computationally efficient via FFT. Main contributions are: (1) a ranked frequency-selection metadescriptor for chunkwise stream characterization, (2) a clustering-based concept identification pipeline for post-hoc analysis and automatic estimation of the number of concepts, and (3) a visualization mechanism that reconstructs selected frequencies into spatial-domain approximations. Expected outcomes are improved unsupervised concept separation on high-dimensional streams relative to PCA and standard meta-feature sets, plus interpretable visual representations of concept signatures. Experiments: Datasets: 1) Synthetic streams generated with controlled drifts: feature dims ∈ {64, 500}, chunks ∈ {50,100,200,256,400}, stream length ∈ {500,1000 chunks}, drift counts ∈ {1,3,5,7,9}, drift dynamics ∈ {sudden, gradual, incremental}. 2) Real-world insects recordings as provided (33 features) using published chunkings. Baselines: (a) PCA (2 components), (b) CED-style meta-features (10 aggregated statistical metafeatures: mean, std, correlation, skewness, kurtosis aggregated by mean/std), (c) ICI-style meta-features (expanded 19-feature set including entropy, Fisher ratio, mutual information, concentration coefficients). Representations: FFM with hyperparameter n ∈ {1,2,4,8,16}; per-sample FFT (real part), average per-chunk, select top-n frequencies by across-chunk variance; normalize and cluster with k-means. Metrics: For labelled synthetic streams use Normalized Mutual Information (NMI), Adjusted Rand Index (ARI), completeness, homogeneity. For unlabeled/real streams use silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz, Davies-Bouldin; additionally report cluster counts. Experimental protocol: Run each stream × method × hyperparameter configuration with 10 independent random seeds; report mean ± std. Statistical tests: paired t-test (α=0.05) comparing FFM (n=8 and n=16) against each baseline. Ablations/Comparisons: (1) Selection strategy ablation: variance-based vs random frequency selection vs PCA-based selection of components; (2) Representation ablation: real-part-only vs magnitude-spectrum vs full complex magnitude; (3) Chunk-size sensitivity: evaluate chunk sizes and report performance vs per-chunk sample count. Additional evaluations: evaluate silhouette-maximization procedure to estimate unknown number of concepts (search k ∈ [2,11]). Implementation details: per-sample FFT cost O(d log d); clustering on normalized top-n vectors; all experiments repeatable and logged. Risk Factors and Limitations: Frequency-domain representation may fail when discriminative signals are nonperiodic or not well represented by Fourier bases (technical failure mode); truncating to real-part or d/2 coefficients can discard relevant phase information and reduce discriminability; method assumes intra-chunk stationarity—if chunks mix multiple rapidly changing sub-concepts the averaged spectrum will blur signals; chunk-size sensitivity: too-small chunks yield noisy frequency estimates, too-large chunks reduce temporal resolution of change points; selection-by-variance can pick components dominated by noise or sensor drift rather than class-relevant structure; clustering stage depends on k-means assumptions (spherical clusters, equal variance) and may misidentify concepts for nonconvex cluster geometry; scalability limits: while FFT per sample is O(d log d), memory and compute scale with number of samples and high d (many chunks × high feature count); evaluation bias: synthetic streams may not capture all real-world nonstationarities, and internal clustering metrics (silhouette, C-H, D-B) have known biases and may not correlate with downstream classifier performance.
